text:
Johannes looked bewilderedly at the man, at his gate, wondering whether he should go in through it or remain standing there, then at the man again, at his long coat, his hat; he smiled in confusion and pain, like someone in distress.

The old tutor continued threateningly:

Another example; can you deny it? Nor did she get the man she was to have, her beloved since childhood, a young, splendid lieutenant. He went hunting one evening, a shot struck him squarely in the forehead and split his head in two. There he lay, a victim of the little caprice God wished to indulge in with him. Victoria, his bride, began to waste away; a worm ate at her, riddled her heart like a sieve; we, her friends, saw it. Then, a few days ago, she went to a gathering at the home of a family named Seier; incidentally, she told me that you too were to have been there, but did not come. In short, at this gathering she exerts herself beyond her strength; memories of her beloved come storming in upon her and make her lively out of defiance; she dances, dances all evening, dances like a mad person. Then she collapses, the floor turns red beneath her; they lift her up, carry her out, drive her home. She did not last long.

The tutor stepped close to Johannes and said harshly:

Victoria is dead.

Just like a blind man, Johannes began to fend the words off with his hands.

Dead? When did she die? Oh, so Victoria is dead?

She is dead, the tutor replied. She died this morning, this very forenoon. He thrust his hand into his pocket and drew out a thick letter. And she entrusted this letter to me to deliver to you. Here it is. After my death, she said. She is dead. I am delivering the letter to you. My mission is ended.

And without a greeting, without saying anything more, the tutor turned around and drifted slowly down the street and disappeared.

Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters, the lines were straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he went in through his gate, up the stairs, found the right key to insert into the door lock, and opened it. His room was cold and dark. He sat down by the window and read Victoria’s letter in the last remnant of daylight.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I shall be dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed before you, and I am writing to you again, as though there were nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was still fully alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than written to you again; but now my soul has begun to leave my body, and I no longer think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung left; what more have I to be bashful about?

I have lain here in bed thinking over the last words I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did not think they would be my last words, for then I would have said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have lain here, both yesterday and today, wishing that I were not too ill to make my way home again and go into the woods and find the place where we sat when you held both my hands; for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find some trace of you and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot come home now unless perhaps I get a little better, as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have done nothing but come to earth and love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe that it is strange to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter of carriages; I suppose I shall never see spring again either, and these houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me. Today I was allowed to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a little while. Down on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and took each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange to me that I, who lay watching this, was to die. I found myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting for my hour; but if they knew it, they would surely still greet each other and speak to each other just as they do now. Last night, when it was dark, I thought it was to be my final moment; my heart began to stand still, and it was as though I could already hear eternity rushing toward me from far away. But the next moment I returned from far away and began to breathe again. It was an utterly indescribable feeling. But Mama thinks that perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Good God, if only you knew how I have loved you, Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has placed itself in my way, first and foremost my own nature. Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter. But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I write to you once more and tell you so. I ask myself why I do it, since it is of no consequence to you, especially when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I wanted so much to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for you as early as two days ago, but I preferred to write. I would also prefer you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were. For that reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I also want to ask you not to see me in my coffin. I am probably much as I was when I lived, only somewhat paler, and I am lying in a yellow dress; but even so, you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and still I have not managed to tell you one thousandth of what I wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to; I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would certainly never be cruel to you again, Johannes. How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat all the paving stones and stop and thank every stair I passed, and be good to everyone. It would not matter how badly I suffered, if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain about anything again; no, I would smile at whoever attacked and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this failed life is to end now. If you knew how unwilling I am to die, then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power. You probably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and never again do harm to anyone, but smile at everything ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.
